title: The silver cup (Genesis 44:1–17)
hook: the test: will the brothers abandon another favorite son?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers come for bread, and bow to a man they don't recognize. Your line was you don't see who it is. Did you look again at someone? Day seventy-two.

The grain runs out, and the brothers have to go back to Egypt. This time they bring Benjamin, because the governor demanded it. Jacob lets him go only after Judah promises: I'll be responsible for him. If I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. In Egypt, the governor invites them to a feast. Simeon is released. Benjamin gets five times as much food as anyone else. The favorite son, again, getting more, right in front of the others. And the brothers seem fine with it. They eat and drink and relax. The next morning they head for home, sacks full. Today: what's hidden in Benjamin's sack.
screen: `THEY BRING BENJAMIN.` → `FIVE TIMES AS MUCH FOR HIM.` → `SACKS FULL, HEADING HOME.`

segments.voice: Before they leave, Joseph gives his steward an order: put my silver cup in the youngest one's sack. They're barely out of the city when the steward catches up. Why have you repaid good with evil? You stole my master's cup! The brothers are so sure of themselves they make a reckless offer: whoever has it, let him die, and the rest of us will be slaves. The steward searches, oldest to youngest. Sack after sack. And it's in Benjamin's. The brothers tear their clothes, the same thing Jacob did over Joseph's coat, and every one of them turns around and goes back to the city. That's the moment. Nobody has to go back. Judah speaks for all of them: "God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants." He doesn't argue about the cup. He's thinking of an older guilt. We'll all be your slaves, he says. Then the governor makes them an easy offer: only the one who had the cup will be my slave. The rest of you, go home in peace. It's the pit all over again. A favored son of Rachel. A chance to be rid of him, and to tell their father something sad but blameless. And not one of them walks away. Maimonides, the great medieval teacher, describes complete repentance, teshuvah, this way. It's when you find yourself in the same situation, with the same pull, the same chance, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't, but because you've changed. The silver cup is that test. Years ago these brothers sold a favorite son. This time they won't.
screen: `A CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.` · `THEY ALL GO BACK.` · `GO HOME IN PEACE; LEAVE HIM.` · `SAME CHANCE, DIFFERENT CHOICE.` · then, large: `NOT THIS TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by someone when it costs you. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who might need you on their side right now. A friend people are talking about. A coworker taking the blame. A family member who's the odd one out. Picture yourself standing next to them. What would it cost you? A little comfort, some awkwardness, a bit of your reputation? Hold that cost honestly. Then decide if you'll pay it. The bell holds the time.
The silver cup. Hidden in Benjamin's sack as a test, to see whether the brothers would abandon another favorite son. They wouldn't.
Your line: not this time. Today, when an old habit shows up, the one you've been trying to leave behind, say those words, and choose differently. Day seventy-two.

howItsDone: Jews call turning around teshuvah; Maimonides' test for it, facing the same situation and choosing differently, is one way teachers read this story.

fork.setup: you're one of the brothers. the governor says: only Benjamin stays as my slave; the rest of you, go home in peace. what do you do?
options: go home. it's not your fault.
fork.reveal: they stay. Judah speaks for them all, and tomorrow he makes an offer that changes everything.

original.note: Hebrew: teshuvah, turning, return. the word for repentance, from shuv, to turn back.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph playing a cruel trick.
what it means: a test built to recreate the pit: a favored son, a way out, and a chance to choose differently.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Laws of Repentance 2:1: complete teshuvah is when the same opportunity returns and you refrain, not from weakness but from change.

notes: 'Twenty-two years' since the sale: Joseph 17 at the sale, 30 before Pharaoh, plus seven good years and two famine years (45:6) = 39. Confirm.
Maimonides, Laws of Repentance 2:1, paraphrased. Confirm.
Judah's pledge (43:9) paraphrased in the hook.
